items.title: Custom Sinks
items.text: Under certain circumstances, it is useful to send the log output to a destination other than a file, stderr and/or stdout. For this purpose, the library provides the nglog::LogSink interface whose implementations can be used to write the log output to arbitrary locations.

items.title: Basic Interface
items.text:
The sink interface is defined as follows:

class LogSink {
 public:
  virtual void send(LogSeverity severity, const char* full_filename,
                    const char* base_filename, int line,
                    const LogMessageTime& time, const char* message,
                    size_t message_len);
};

The user must implement nglog::LogSink::send, which is called by the library every time a message is logged.

Sink callbacks may run concurrently for different messages. They must be thread-safe and may use LOG() or CHECK() for nested logging.

Callbacks for the sinks associated with one message retain the library's existing sink order. No ordering is guaranteed between callbacks for different messages.

items.title: Registering Log Sinks
items.text:
To use the custom sink and instance of the above interface implementation must be registered using nglog::AddLogSink which expects a pointer to the nglog::LogSink instance. To unregister use nglog::RemoveLogSink. Both functions are thread-safe.

LogSink ownership

The nglog::LogSink instance must not be destroyed until the referencing pointer is unregistered.

items.title: Direct Logging
items.text:
Instead of registering the sink, we can directly use to log messages. While LOG_TO_SINK(sink, severity) allows to log both to the sink and to a global log registry, e.g., a file, LOG_TO_SINK_BUT_NOT_TO_LOGFILE(sink, severity) will avoid the latter.

Using a custom sink

custom_sink.cc
void WriteUsage(nglog::HelpWriter& help) {
  help.Write(nglog::HelpTextStyle::kHeading, "Usage:");
  help.Write(" ");
  help.Write(nglog::HelpTextStyle::kExecutable, "custom_sink_example");
  help.Write(" ");
  help.Write(nglog::HelpTextStyle::kUsageOptions, "[options]");
  help.Write("\n\nWrites log messages to ");
  help.Write(nglog::HelpTextStyle::kStream, "stdout");
  help.Write(" through a custom sink. Use ");
  help.Write(nglog::HelpTextStyle::kOptionPrefix, "--");
  help.Write(nglog::HelpTextStyle::kOption, "logtostderr");
  help.Write("=");
  help.Write(nglog::HelpTextStyle::kConstant, "true");
  help.Write(" to route ng-log output to ");
  help.Write(nglog::HelpTextStyle::kStream, "stderr");
  help.Write(".\n");
}

}  // namespace

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  nglog::SetUsageMessage(WriteUsage);
  nglog::ParseCommandLineFlags(&argc, &argv,
                               nglog::FlagParsingMode::kRemoveFlags);
  nglog::InitializeLogging(argv[0]);

  MyLogSink sink;
  nglog::AddLogSink(&sink);  // (2)!

  LOG(INFO) << "logging to MySink";

  nglog::RemoveLogSink(&sink);  // (3)!

  // We can directly log to a sink without registering it
  LOG_TO_SINK(&sink, INFO) << "direct logging";  // (4)!
  LOG_TO_SINK_BUT_NOT_TO_LOGFILE(&sink, INFO)
      << "direct logging but not to file";
}
  1. MySink implements a custom sink that sends log messages to std::cout.
  2. The custom sink must be registered to for use with existing logging macros.
  3. Once the custom sink is no longer needed we remove it from the registry.
  4. A sink does not need to be registered globally. However, then, messages must be logged using dedicated macros.

Running the above example as NGLOG_log_dir=. ./custom_sink_example will produce

Custom sink output
INFO custom_sink.cc:63 logging to MySink
INFO custom_sink.cc:68 direct logging
INFO custom_sink.cc:69 direct logging but not to file (1)
  1. This line is not present in the log file because we used LOG_TO_SINK_BUT_NOT_TO_LOGFILE to log the message.

and the corresponding log file will contain

Log file generated with the custom sink
Log file created at: 2024/06/11 13:24:27
Running on machine: pc
Running duration (h:mm:ss): 0:00:00
Log line format: [IWEF]yyyymmdd hh:mm:ss.uuuuuu threadid file:line] msg
I20240611 13:24:27.476620 126237946035776 custom_sink.cc:63] logging to MySink
I20240611 13:24:27.476796 126237946035776 custom_sink.cc:68] direct logging

items.title: Installation Notes for 64-bit Linux Systems
items.text:
Note

The description on this page is possibly not up-to-date.

The glibc built-in stack-unwinder on 64-bit systems has some problems with ng-log. In particular, if you are using InstallFailureSignalHandler(), the signal may be raised in the middle of malloc, holding some malloc-related locks when they invoke the stack unwinder. The built-in stack unwinder may call malloc recursively, which may require the thread to acquire a lock it already holds resulting in a deadlock.

items.title: Recommended Approach: libunwind
items.text:
For above reason, if you use a 64-bit system and you need InstallFailureSignalHandler(), we strongly recommend you install libunwind before trying to configure or install ng-log. libunwind can be found here.

Even if you already have libunwind installed, you will probably still need to install from the snapshot to get the latest version.

Warning

If you install libunwind from the URL above, be aware that you may have trouble if you try to statically link your binary with ng-log: that is, if you link with gcc -static -lgcc_eh .... This is because both libunwind and libgcc implement the same C++ exception handling APIs, but they implement them differently on some platforms. This is not likely to be a problem on ia64, but may be on x86-64.

Also, if you link binaries statically, make sure that you add -Wl,--eh-frame-hdr to your linker options. This is required so that libunwind can find the information generated by the compiler required for stack unwinding.

Using -static is rare, though, so unless you know this will affect you it probably won't.

items.title: Alternative Stack-unwinder
items.text: If you cannot or do not wish to install libunwind, you can still try to use two kinds of stack-unwinder:

items.title: glibc Built-in Stack-unwinder
items.text: As we already mentioned, glibc's unwinder has a deadlock issue. However, if you don't use InstallFailureSignalHandler() or you don't worry about the rare possibilities of deadlocks, you can use this stack-unwinder. If you specify no options and libunwind isn't detected on your system, the configure script chooses this unwinder by default.

items.title: Frame Pointer based Stack-unwinder
items.text: The frame pointer based stack unwinder requires that your application, the ng-log library, and system libraries like libc, all be compiled with a frame pointer. This is not the default for x86-64.

items.title: Using ng-log in a CMake Project
items.text:
Assuming that ng-log was previously built using CMake or installed using a package manager, you can use the CMake command find_package to build against ng-log in your CMake project as follows:

CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required (VERSION 3.28)
project (myproj VERSION 1.0)

find_package (ng-log 0.9.0 REQUIRED)

add_executable (myapp main.cpp)
target_link_libraries (myapp ng-log::ng-log)

Compile definitions and options will be added automatically to your target as needed.

Alternatively, ng-log can be incorporated into using the CMake command add_subdirectory to include ng-log directly from a subdirectory of your project by replacing the find_package call from the previous snippet by add_subdirectory. The ng-log::ng-log target is in this case an ALIAS library target for the ng-log library target.

items.title: File and directory paths
items.text:
All file and directory paths passed to ng-log must use UTF-8 encoding. This includes logfile destinations, log directories, and paths passed to TruncateLogFile.

ng-log uses narrow C runtime filesystem operations for ASCII paths that remain shorter than MAX_PATH after resolving them against the current directory, unless they start with the \\?\ or \\.\ namespace prefix. Other paths are converted to UTF-16. Directory enumeration uses Unicode Windows APIs so every entry name can be represented. Invalid UTF-8 paths are rejected. This behavior is consistent with the other supported platforms and does not require a change to the public API.

items.title: Compiler character sets
items.text:
ng-log expects narrow string arguments to contain UTF-8 bytes. With MSVC, use /utf-8 when source files are stored as UTF-8 and ordinary narrow string literals must also be encoded as UTF-8. This option is equivalent to /source-charset:utf-8 /execution-charset:utf-8. These options enable /validate-charset by default.

Use /source-charset:utf-8 by itself only when MSVC must read the source as UTF-8 but the program intentionally uses another execution character set. Non-ASCII ordinary narrow string literals produced by such a build are not necessarily valid ng-log input.

Use /execution-charset:utf-8 by itself when the source encoding is already identified correctly, such as by a byte-order mark or another compiler option, and ordinary narrow string literals must be UTF-8. For UTF-8 source files without a byte-order mark, also specify /source-charset:utf-8 or use /utf-8.

These options affect source decoding and compile-time string literals. They do not convert runtime text obtained from files, environment variables, or other APIs. Applications must convert such text to UTF-8 before passing it to ng-log. ASCII input is valid UTF-8.

items.title: Long paths
items.text:
ng-log supports file and directory paths longer than MAX_PATH without requiring callers to add an extended-length path prefix. Relative paths, drive paths, and UNC paths are converted to absolute extended-length paths when necessary. Paths that already use an extended-length or device prefix are preserved.

The short ASCII fast path is unchanged. It avoids UTF-16 conversion and path normalization while a path remains below MAX_PATH. The length of a relative path includes the current directory it is resolved against, so a short relative path inside a deep directory is also treated as a long path. Longer paths use the Unicode path handling described above. Individual path components and the complete path remain subject to the limits of the underlying Windows file system.

Long-path normalization uses the Windows PathCch API. As a result, ng-log now requires Windows 8 or Windows Server 2012 or later.

items.title: Log output
items.text: Log messages are expected to use UTF-8. When standard output or standard error is connected to a Windows console, an ASCII fast path writes messages directly to the console handle without converting them to UTF-16. Messages containing non-ASCII characters are converted to UTF-16 and written with the Unicode console API. Redirected output is written as UTF-8 through the stream's existing translation mode, so a text-mode stream translates line feeds into CRLF sequences exactly like the application's own output. Ill-formed UTF-8 sequences are replaced with U+FFFD when writing to the console or the debugger. Debugger output uses the corresponding Unicode debugger API.

items.title: Log file links
items.text: On other platforms, ng-log creates a symbolic link to the latest log file of each severity. On Windows, it creates a shell shortcut named <basename>.<severity>.lnk instead, because creating symbolic links requires elevated privileges or developer mode. The log_link flag places an additional shortcut in the given directory.

items.title: Severity levels
items.text:
ng-log defines the severity level ERROR, which is also defined by windows.h. You can make nglog not define INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and FATAL by defining NGLOG_NO_ABBREVIATED_SEVERITIES before including nglog/logging.h. The prefixed constants NGLOG_INFO, NGLOG_WARNING, NGLOG_ERROR, and NGLOG_FATAL are always available in the global namespace.

Even with this macro, you can still use the iostream like logging facilities:

#define NGLOG_NO_ABBREVIATED_SEVERITIES
#include <windows.h>
#include <ng-log/logging.h>

// ...

LOG(ERROR) << "This should work";
LOG_IF(ERROR, x > y) << "This should be also OK";

However, you cannot use INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and FATAL anymore for functions defined in nglog/logging.h.

#define NGLOG_NO_ABBREVIATED_SEVERITIES
#include <windows.h>
#include <ng-log/logging.h>

// ...

// This won’t work.
// nglog::FlushLogFiles(nglog::ERROR);

// Use this instead.
nglog::FlushLogFiles(NGLOG_ERROR);

If you don't need ERROR defined by windows.h, there are a couple of more workarounds which sometimes don't work1:

  • #define WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN or NOGDI before #include <windows.h>.
  • #undef ERROR after #include <windows.h>.

  1. For more information refer to this issue. ↩

items.title: Logging
items.text:
ng-log defines a series of macros that simplify many common logging tasks. You can log messages by severity level, control logging behavior from the command line, log based on conditionals, abort the program when expected conditions are not met, introduce your own logging levels, customize the prefix attached to log messages, and more.

Planned deprecation

The experimental logging functions are planned to supersede the macros in ng-log 0.10.0, after which the macros would be deprecated and eventually removed. Nothing is deprecated yet and the plan may change.

items.title: Severity Levels
items.text:
You can specify one of the following severity levels (in increasing order of severity):

  1. INFO,
  2. WARNING,
  3. ERROR, and
  4. FATAL.

Logging a FATAL message terminates the program (after the message is logged).

Note

Messages of a given severity are logged not only to corresponding severity logfile but also to other logfiles of lower severity. For instance, a message of severity FATAL will be logged to logfiles of severity FATAL, ERROR, WARNING, and INFO.

The DFATAL severity logs a FATAL error in debug mode (i.e., there is no NDEBUG macro defined), but avoids halting the program in production by automatically reducing the severity to ERROR.

items.title: Log Files
items.text:
Unless otherwise specified, ng-log uses the format

<tmp>/<program name>.<hostname>.<user name>.log.<severity level>.<date>-<time>.<pid>

for log filenames written to a directory designated as <tmp> and determined according to the following rules.

Windows

ng-log uses the GetTempPathW API function to retrieve the directory for temporary files with a fallback to

  1. C:\TMP\
  2. C:\TEMP\

(in the order given.)

All file and directory path arguments passed to ng-log must be encoded as UTF-8. On Windows, ASCII paths without a namespace prefix that remain shorter than MAX_PATH after resolving them against the current directory use narrow C runtime filesystem operations. Other paths use Unicode filesystem APIs. Invalid UTF-8 paths are rejected. Directory enumeration uses Unicode Windows APIs so every entry name can be represented. MSVC users should also review the compiler character set guidance when non-ASCII filenames appear in source files or narrow string literals. This support requires Windows 8 or Windows Server 2012 or later.

Log messages also use UTF-8. On Windows, an ASCII fast path writes console output directly to the console handle without converting it to UTF-16. Output containing non-ASCII characters is converted to UTF-16 and written with Unicode console APIs. Redirected output remains UTF-8. Debugger output uses the Unicode debugger API. MSVC users should also review the compiler character set guidance when non-ASCII text appears in source files or narrow string literals.

non-Windows

The directory is determined by referencing the environment variables

  1. TMPDIR
  2. TMP

if set with a fallback to /tmp/.

On POSIX systems with descriptor-relative filesystem APIs, ng-log supports log paths longer than the complete pathname limit reported by PATH_MAX. Ordinary paths use the direct filesystem operation as a fast path. If that operation fails with ENAMETOOLONG, ng-log resolves the directory components through file descriptors and retries the operation relative to the containing directory. Individual path components and symbolic link targets remain subject to the limits of the underlying filesystem. Emscripten emulates descriptor-relative operations through complete pathnames, so the limit still applies there.

The default path to a log file on Linux, for instance, could be

/tmp/hello_world.example.com.hamaji.log.INFO.20080709-222411.10474

By default, ng-log echos ERROR and FATAL messages to standard error in addition to log files.

items.title: Log Line Prefix Format
items.text:
Log lines have this form:

Lyyyymmdd hh:mm:ss.uuuuuu threadid file:line] msg...

where the fields are defined as follows:

Placeholder Meaning L A single character, representing the log level (e.g., I for INFO) yyyy The year mm The month (zero padded; i.e., May is 05) dd The day (zero padded) hh:mm:ss.uuuuuu Time in hours, minutes and fractional seconds threadid The space-padded thread ID file The file name line The line number msg The user-supplied message

Default log line prefix format

I1103 11:57:31.739339 24395 nglog.cc:2341] Command line: ./some_prog
I1103 11:57:31.739403 24395 nglog.cc:2342] Process id 24395

Note

Although microseconds are useful for comparing events on a single machine, clocks on different machines may not be well synchronized. Hence, use with caution when comparing the low bits of timestamps from different machines.

items.title: Format Customization
items.text:
The predefined log line prefix can be replaced using a user-provided callback that formats the corresponding output.

For each log entry, the callback will be invoked with a reference to a nglog::LogMessage instance containing the severity, filename, line number, thread ID, and time of the event. It will also be given a reference to the output stream, whose contents will be prepended to the actual message in the final log line.

To enable the use of a prefix formatter, use the

nglog::InstallPrefixFormatter(&MyPrefixFormatter);

function to pass a pointer to the corresponding MyPrefixFormatter callback during initialization. InstallPrefixFormatter takes a second optional argument of type void* that allows supplying user data to the callback.

Custom prefix formatter

The following function outputs a prefix that matches ng-log's default format. The third parameter data can be used to access user-supplied data which unless specified defaults to nullptr.

void MyPrefixFormatter(std::ostream& s, const nglog::LogMessage& m, void* /*data*/) {
   s << nglog::GetLogSeverityName(m.severity())[0]
   << setw(4) << 1900 + m.time().year()
   << setw(2) << 1 + m.time().month()
   << setw(2) << m.time().day()
   << ' '
   << setw(2) << m.time().hour() << ':'
   << setw(2) << m.time().min()  << ':'
   << setw(2) << m.time().sec() << "."
   << setw(6) << m.time().usec()
   << ' '
   << setfill(' ') << setw(5)
   << m.thread_id() << setfill('0')
   << ' '
   << m.basename() << ':' << m.line() << "]";
}

items.title: Conditional / Occasional Logging
items.text:
Sometimes, you may only want to log a message under certain conditions. You can use the following macros to perform conditional logging:

LOG_IF(INFO, num_cookies > 10) << "Got lots of cookies";

The "Got lots of cookies" message is logged only when the variable num_cookies exceeds 10. If a line of code is executed many times, it may be useful to only log a message at certain intervals. This kind of logging is most useful for informational messages.

LOG_EVERY_N(INFO, 10) << "Got the " << nglog::COUNTER << "th cookie";

The above line outputs a log messages on the 1st, 11th, 21st, ... times it is executed.

Note

The placeholder nglog::COUNTER identifies the recurring repetition.

You can combine conditional and occasional logging with the following macro.

LOG_IF_EVERY_N(INFO, (size > 1024), 10) << "Got the " << nglog::COUNTER
                                        << "th big cookie";

Instead of outputting a message every nth time, you can also limit the output to the first n occurrences:

LOG_FIRST_N(INFO, 20) << "Got the " << nglog::COUNTER << "th cookie";

Outputs log messages for the first 20 times it is executed. The nglog::COUNTER identifier indicates which repetition is happening.

Other times, it is desired to only log a message periodically based on a time. For instance, to log a message every 10ms:

LOG_EVERY_T(INFO, 0.01) << "Got a cookie";

Or every 2.35s:

LOG_EVERY_T(INFO, 2.35) << "Got a cookie";

items.title: Verbose Logging
items.text:
When you are chasing difficult bugs, thorough log messages are very useful. However, you may want to ignore too verbose messages in usual development. For such verbose logging, ng-log provides the VLOG macro, which allows you to define your own numeric logging levels.

The --v command line option controls which verbose messages are logged:

VLOG(1) << "I’m printed when you run the program with --v=1 or higher";
VLOG(2) << "I’m printed when you run the program with --v=2 or higher";

With VLOG, the lower the verbose level, the more likely messages are to be logged. For example, if --v=1, VLOG(1) will log, but VLOG(2) will not log.

Warning

The VLOG behavior is opposite of the severity level logging, where INFO, ERROR, etc. are defined in increasing order and thus --minloglevel of 1 will only log WARNING and above.

Though you can specify any integers for both VLOG macro and --v flag, the common values for them are small positive integers. For example, if you write VLOG(0), you should specify --v=-1 or lower to silence it. This is less useful since we may not want verbose logs by default in most cases. The VLOG macros always log at the INFO log level (when they log at all).

Verbose logging can be controlled from the command line on a per-module basis:

--vmodule=mapreduce=2,file=1,gfs*=3 --v=0

Specifying these options will specifically:

  1. Print VLOG(2) and lower messages from source files whose base is mapreduce
  2. Print VLOG(1) and lower messages from source files whose base is file
  3. Print VLOG(3) and lower messages from source files whose base starts with gfs
  4. Print VLOG(0) and lower messages from elsewhere

The module name is matched against the source filename base, which is the part before the first period. A trailing -inl suffix is removed before matching. The wildcard patterns support both * (matches 0 or more characters) and ? (matches any single character). Please also refer to command line flags for more information.

There's also VLOG_IS_ON(n) "verbose level" condition macro. This macro returns true when the effective verbose level from --v or the applicable --vmodule entry is equal to or greater than n. The macro can be used as follows:

if (VLOG_IS_ON(2)) {
    // (1)
}
  1. Here we can perform some logging preparation and logging that can’t be accomplished with just VLOG(2) << "message ...";

Verbose level condition macros VLOG_IF, VLOG_EVERY_N and VLOG_IF_EVERY_N behave analogous to LOG_IF, LOG_EVERY_N, LOG_IF_EVERY_N, but accept a numeric verbosity level as opposed to a severity level.

VLOG_IF(1, (size > 1024))
   << "I’m printed when size is more than 1024 and when you run the "
      "program with --v=1 or more";
VLOG_EVERY_N(1, 10)
   << "I’m printed every 10th occurrence, and when you run the program "
      "with --v=1 or more. Present occurrence is " << nglog::COUNTER;
VLOG_IF_EVERY_N(1, (size > 1024), 10)
   << "I’m printed on every 10th occurrence of case when size is more "
      " than 1024, when you run the program with --v=1 or more. ";
      "Present occurrence is " << nglog::COUNTER;

Performance

The conditional logging macros provided by nglog (e.g., CHECK, LOG_IF, VLOG, etc.) are carefully implemented and don't execute the right hand side expressions when the conditions are false. So, the following check may not sacrifice the performance of your application.

CHECK(obj.ok) << obj.CreatePrettyFormattedStringButVerySlow();

items.title: Debugging Support
items.text:
Special debug mode logging macros only have an effect in debug mode and are compiled away to nothing for non-debug mode compiles. Use these macros to avoid slowing down your production application due to excessive logging.

DLOG(INFO) << "Found cookies";
DLOG_IF(INFO, num_cookies > 10) << "Got lots of cookies";
DLOG_EVERY_N(INFO, 10) << "Got the " << nglog::COUNTER << "th cookie";
DLOG_FIRST_N(INFO, 10) << "Got the " << nglog::COUNTER << "th cookie";
DLOG_EVERY_T(INFO, 0.01) << "Got a cookie";

items.title: Runtime Checks
items.text:
It is a good practice to check expected conditions in your program frequently to detect errors as early as possible. The CHECK macro provides the ability to abort the application when a condition is not met, similar to the assert macro defined in the standard C library.

CHECK aborts the application if a condition is not true. Unlike assert, it is not controlled by NDEBUG, so the check will be executed regardless of compilation mode. Therefore, fp->Write(x) in the following example is always executed:

CHECK(fp->Write(x) == 4) << "Write failed!";

There are various helper macros for equality/inequality checks -CHECK_EQ, CHECK_NE, CHECK_LE, CHECK_LT, CHECK_GE, and CHECK_GT. They compare two values, and log a FATAL message including the two values when the result is not as expected. The values must have operator<<(ostream, ...) defined.

You may append to the error message like so:

CHECK_NE(1, 2) << ": The world must be ending!";

We are very careful to ensure that each argument is evaluated exactly once, and that anything which is legal to pass as a function argument is legal here. In particular, the arguments may be temporary expressions which will end up being destroyed at the end of the apparent statement, for example:

CHECK_EQ(string("abc")[1], ’b’);

The compiler reports an error if one of the arguments is a pointer and the other is nullptr. To work around this, simply static_cast nullptr to the type of the desired pointer.

CHECK_EQ(some_ptr, static_cast<SomeType*>(nullptr));

Better yet, use the CHECK_NOTNULL macro:

CHECK_NOTNULL(some_ptr);
some_ptr->DoSomething();

Since this macro returns the given pointer, this is very useful in constructor initializer lists.

struct S {
    S(Something* ptr) : ptr_(CHECK_NOTNULL(ptr)) {}
    Something* ptr_;
};

Warning

Due to the argument forwarding, CHECK_NOTNULL cannot be used to simultaneously stream an additional custom message. To provide a custom message, one can use the macro CHECK_EQ prior to the failing check.

If you are comparing C strings (char *), a handy set of macros performs both case sensitive and insensitive comparisons - CHECK_STREQ, CHECK_STRNE, CHECK_STRCASEEQ, and CHECK_STRCASENE. The CHECK_*CASE* macro variants are case-insensitive. You can safely pass nullptr pointers to this macro. They treat nullptr and any non-nullptr string as not equal. Two nullptrs are equal.

Note

Both arguments may be temporary objects which are destructed at the end of the current full expression, such as

CHECK_STREQ(Foo().c_str(), Bar().c_str());

where Foo and Bar return std::string.

The CHECK_DOUBLE_EQ macro checks the equality of two floating point values, accepting a small error margin. CHECK_NEAR accepts a third floating point argument, which specifies the acceptable error margin.

items.title: Raw Logging
items.text: The header file <ng-log/raw_logging.h> can be used for thread-safe logging, which does not allocate any memory or acquire any locks. Therefore, the macros defined in this header file can be used by low-level memory allocation and synchronization code. Please check src/ng-log/raw_logging.h for detail.

items.title: Library Style perror()
items.text:
PLOG() and PLOG_IF() and PCHECK() behave exactly like their LOG* and CHECK equivalents with the addition that they append a description of the current state of errno to their output lines. E.g.

PCHECK(write(1, nullptr, 2) >= 0) << "Write nullptr failed";

This check fails with the following error message.

F0825 185142 test.cc:22] Check failed: write(1, nullptr, 2) >= 0 Write nullptr failed: Bad address [14]

items.title: Syslog
items.text: SYSLOG, SYSLOG_IF, and SYSLOG_EVERY_N macros are available. These log to syslog in addition to the normal logs. Be aware that logging to syslog can drastically impact performance, especially if syslog is configured for remote logging! Make sure you understand the implications of outputting to syslog before you use these macros. In general, it's wise to use these macros sparingly.

items.title: Experimental Logging API
items.text:
Experimental

API and ABI may change or be removed in any release without notice.

The experimental logging functions format messages with std::format and capture the call site with std::source_location. They share the implementation of the logging macros, so their output is identical.

Planned replacement of the macros

The functions are planned to supersede the macros in ng-log 0.10.0, after which the macros would be deprecated and eventually removed. Nothing is deprecated yet and the plan may change. See Migrating from the Macros.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
The functions require C++20 or newer with compile-time checked std::format strings, std::source_location and constexpr std::string and are built whenever the compiler provides them. The rest of the library requires C++14 only. If a requirement is missing, the header fails with a single diagnostic that names it. Configuring with -DWITH_EXPERIMENTAL=OFF omits the functions even if the compiler supports them and does not install their headers. The headers in a build tree, such as with add_subdirectory, then fail to compile with a diagnostic that says so.

The functions are opt-in. Include the umbrella header or only the headers needed and compile the using translation units as C++20 or newer:

Including the functions
#include <ng-log/experimental/logging.h>

namespace ngx = nglog::experimental;
Header Contents ng-log/experimental/logging.h All of the headers below, ng-log/log_setup.h and ng-log/log_sink.h ng-log/experimental/attributes.h Attributes and custom attributes ng-log/experimental/format.h The format string and Lazy ng-log/experimental/log_call.h Log, which the next two headers enable for their destinations, and IsDebugEnabled ng-log/experimental/log.h The regular destinations of Log and Ensure, and IsEnabled ng-log/experimental/signal_safe_log.h The SignalSafe destination of Log and Ensure ng-log/experimental/ensure.h Ensure, comparisons, That, NGLOG_COMPARE and NotNull ng-log/experimental/sink.h Structured sinks

log.h, signal_safe_log.h and ensure.h include log_call.h, attributes.h and format.h. Log and Ensure write to the regular destinations only if log.h is included and to the signal-safe one only if signal_safe_log.h is. The examples below include the headers they use.

None of these headers defines unprefixed macros such as LOG, CHECK or VLOG. A translation unit can therefore use the functions together with another logging library that defines the same names, such as Abseil Logging, as long as it does not include the headers of the macros, ng-log/logging.h, ng-log/raw_logging.h and ng-log/vlog_is_on.h.

The experimental component of the CMake package provides the ng-log::experimental target, which links ng-log and compiles its consumers as C++20 or newer. The component is available if ng-log was built with the functions and the compiler of the consuming project supports them as well, which find_package checks. Requiring the component otherwise fails with the reason. Without components or with the component requested as optional, the target is provided whenever the component is available, and ng-log_experimental_FOUND tells whether it is:

Linking the functions in CMake
find_package (ng-log 0.9.0 REQUIRED COMPONENTS experimental)

target_link_libraries (myapp PRIVATE ng-log::experimental)

If ng-log is added using add_subdirectory, the target exists only if the functions were built, which if (TARGET ng-log::experimental) determines.

items.title: Functions
items.text:
Log(attributes, format, args...)

Logs a message described by attributes.

Log{attributes, format, args...}

Same as above, but evaluates the attributes before the arguments, except with MSVC. See argument evaluation order.

Log(attributes)(format, args...)

Two-stage form of the above, which also evaluates the attributes before the arguments.

Log(format, args...)

Logs an Info message.

Log(condition, [attributes,] format, args...)

Logs only if the condition holds, like LOG_IF. The condition must be a bool, so pointers and integers need an explicit comparison. Prefer an if statement, which also skips evaluating the arguments. See conditions.

Ensure(condition, [attributes,] format, args...)

Terminates with Check failed: followed by the message unless the condition holds. Accepts all attributes except a severity.

Ensure(comparison, [attributes,] [format, args...])

Terminates with the description of a failed comparison or NotNull check followed by the message, which is optional since the description identifies the failure. Returns the operand of That or NotNull.

IsEnabled(attributes)

Returns whether the attributes admit a message at the call site. Runs only the Configure and Admit hooks and ignores the minimum log level and stripping. Rejects rate limits at compile time, since evaluating them would count an occurrence.

IsDebugEnabled()

Returns at compile time whether debug mode is on in the calling translation unit like DCHECK_IS_ON(), such as to skip expensive code with if constexpr.

Format strings are checked at compile time:

Logging and checking
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>
#include <ng-log/experimental/ensure.h>

ngx::Log("Found {} cookies", num_cookies);
ngx::Log(ngx::Warning, "Disk {} is {}% full", name, usage);
ngx::Ensure(fd >= 0, ngx::Errno, "fd >= 0 Cannot open {}", path);

Argument evaluation order

An argument such as f() may change errno before Errno captures it, since C++ leaves the evaluation order of arguments unspecified. The two-stage form ngx::Log(attributes)(format, args...) captures it first. Ensure has no such form. See argument evaluation order.

items.title: Conditions
items.text:
Log conditionally with an if statement, which skips the arguments as well:

Logging conditionally
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

if (retries > kMaxRetries) {
  ngx::Log(ngx::Warning, "Giving up after {}", Describe(attempts));
}

A condition passed to Log logs the same message but evaluates the arguments regardless, so Describe(attempts) runs even if the condition does not hold:

Logging with a condition argument
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

ngx::Log(retries > kMaxRetries, ngx::Warning, "Giving up after {}",
         Describe(attempts));

A check cannot do without its condition. As with any function call, the arguments of Ensure are evaluated even if the check passes. Defer expensive arguments of both with Lazy.

items.title: Comparisons
items.text:
Comparisons describe the failure like the CHECK_EQ family, including both operands. That wraps the left operand of a comparison using ==, !=, <, <=, > or >= and covers every comparison of the macros:

Checking comparisons
#include <ng-log/experimental/ensure.h>
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(a) == b, "msg {}", x);
// Check failed: lhs == rhs (1 vs. 2) msg 3

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(s1) == s2);
// CHECK_STREQ failed: lhs == rhs (abc vs. abd)

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(s1).IgnoreCase() != s2);
// CHECK_STRCASENE failed: lhs != rhs (abc vs. ABC)

ngx::Ensure(NGLOG_COMPARE(a == b), "msg {}", x);
// Check failed: a == b (1 vs. 2) msg 3

Since a function cannot capture the expression, a failure of That names the operator but not the operands. The log line names the file and line of the check instead. The left operand may contain any operator, such as ngx::That(a + b * 2) == c or ngx::That(x > 0 && y > 0) == true. A right operand containing an operator that binds weaker than comparisons, such as && or ?:, must be parenthesized. Otherwise the check is rejected at compile time, as is That without a comparison.

Unlike CHECK_EQ, That compares C strings, char pointers and arrays, by their contents like CHECK_STREQ. AsPointer compares any pointer by address instead, such as ngx::That(s).AsPointer() == t, and prints both addresses on failure. IgnoreCase compares C strings ignoring case like CHECK_STRCASEEQ. C strings cannot be ordered, and C strings of other character types such as wchar_t cannot be compared, since comparing their addresses is rarely intended. Both are rejected at compile time in favor of std::basic_string_view operands.

Near checks like CHECK_NEAR that the operand lies within a margin of a value, and without a margin like CHECK_DOUBLE_EQ. Unlike the macros, which expand to two checks, it evaluates each operand once and reports both bounds:

Checking ranges
#include <ng-log/experimental/ensure.h>
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(x).Near(y, 0.1));
// Check failed: lhs near rhs (1.5 vs. 1 +/- 0.1)

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(i).IndexOf(a));
// Check failed: lhs index of rhs (5 vs. size 3)

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(x).InRange(0.0, 1.0));
// Check failed: lhs in range (1.5 vs. [0, 1))

IndexOf checks like CHECK_INDEX that an integer is a valid index of an array, a container or any other range whose size is known. BoundOf also admits the size like CHECK_BOUND, such as for the end of a subrange. A negative integer fails both. InRange checks the half-open range [low, high) of any ordered values. Integers compare by value regardless of their signedness.

Comparing a raw, member or smart pointer with nullptr using != checks like CHECK_NOTNULL. Like CHECK_NOTNULL, Ensure returns the operand of any comparison created by That, an lvalue by reference and an rvalue by value, so the check can initialize members. That holds a reference to an lvalue and takes ownership of an rvalue, so a stored operand must not outlive what an lvalue operand refers to. The comparison moves the operand into its result, so a stored operand is compared by moving it. A bit-field cannot be referenced, so it is passed as a value, such as ngx::That(+flags.ready) == 1:

Checking operands in an initializer
#include <ng-log/experimental/ensure.h>
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

Widget::Widget(std::unique_ptr<Engine> engine, std::string name)
    : engine_{ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(std::move(engine)) != nullptr)},
      name_{ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(std::move(name)) != "")} {}
// Check failed: lhs != rhs (0 vs. nullptr)

NGLOG_COMPARE captures the text of the expression instead, so the failure names the operands exactly like CHECK_EQ. Use it if the message must identify the operands or match the output of the macros, such as while migrating. NGLOG_COMPARE(a == b) is equivalent to ngx::Eq(a, b, "a == b"). The left operand may contain arithmetic, such as NGLOG_COMPARE(a + b * 2 == c). Shifts in the left operand and operators that bind weaker than comparisons in either operand, such as &&, ||, & and ?:, must be parenthesized. Otherwise the expression is rejected at compile time, as is one without a comparison or with a comma. Three-way comparisons cannot be checked, since their result compares only with a literal zero, so check std::is_lt(a <=> b) and its siblings as a condition instead. Like CHECK_EQ, == compares C strings by address.

The macros map to That and to functions that, like the macros, take the text to print:

Comparison Macro equivalent That(a) == b and the other operators, NGLOG_COMPARE(a == b) CHECK_EQ(a, b) and its siblings That(s1) == s2, That(s1) != s2 CHECK_STREQ, CHECK_STRNE That(s1).IgnoreCase() == s2, That(s1).IgnoreCase() != s2 CHECK_STRCASEEQ, CHECK_STRCASENE That(p) != nullptr CHECK_NOTNULL That(x).Near(y, m), That(x).Near(y) CHECK_NEAR, CHECK_DOUBLE_EQ That(i).IndexOf(a), That(b).BoundOf(a) CHECK_INDEX, CHECK_BOUND Eq, Ne, Lt, Le, Gt, Ge CHECK_EQ, CHECK_NE, CHECK_LT, CHECK_LE, CHECK_GT, CHECK_GE StrEq, StrNe CHECK_STREQ, CHECK_STRNE StrCaseEq, StrCaseNe CHECK_STRCASEEQ, CHECK_STRCASENE NotNull CHECK_NOTNULL

Operands are rendered like the macros render them if both support << and with std::format otherwise. Unlike the macros, integers of mixed signedness compare by value, so Lt(-1, 1u, "-1 < 1u") holds. String comparisons take C strings. Like the macros, null equals only null and prints as empty.

NotNull accepts raw, member and smart pointers. Wrappers such as std::optional are rejected, since an empty one compares unequal to nullptr. Unlike CHECK_NOTNULL, NotNull also rejects function wrappers such as std::function, which are no pointers. Check them as a condition instead, such as ngx::Ensure(static_cast<bool>(callback), "callback"). ngx::Ensure(ngx::NotNull(std::move(engine), "engine")) fails with Check failed: 'engine' Must be non nullptr.

items.title: Constant Evaluation
items.text:
All functions except IsEnabled can be called in constexpr functions. During constant evaluation, logging has no effect and a failed check is a compile error that names EnsureFailedDuringConstantEvaluation:

Checking during constant evaluation
#include <ng-log/experimental/ensure.h>
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

constexpr int Divide(int a, int b) {
  ngx::Ensure(ngx::Ne(b, 0, "b != 0"));
  return a / b;
}

static_assert(Divide(6, 3) == 2, "Divide must work in constant expressions");
constexpr int kInvalid = Divide(1, 0);  // does not compile

Checks with Debug are skipped if debug mode is off. During constant evaluation, comparisons describe a failure by the expression text only, and case-insensitive string comparisons consider ASCII letters only.

items.title: Signal-Safe Logging
items.text:
With the SignalSafe attribute, Log and Ensure are designed for signal handlers and low-level code. Like RAW_LOG, whose format and implementation they share, they write to stderr and neither allocate nor acquire locks, with the exceptions described below. A failed signal-safe check writes Check failed: before the message:

Logging without allocating
#include <ng-log/experimental/ensure.h>
#include <ng-log/experimental/signal_safe_log.h>

ngx::Log(ngx::SignalSafe | ngx::Error, "read failed with {} on fd {}", result,
         fd);
// E00000000 00:00:00.000000  1234 file.cc:42] RAW: read failed with -1 on fd 3

ngx::Ensure(fd >= 0, ngx::SignalSafe, "bad fd {}", fd);
// F00000000 00:00:00.000000  1234 file.cc:45] RAW: Check failed: bad fd -1

To guarantee that formatting neither allocates nor locks, SignalSafe rejects at compile time:

  • arguments other than integers, floating-point numbers, characters, bool, void pointers, nullptr, C strings, std::string_view and std::string
  • the locale-specific option L
  • attributes other than a severity, Debug and Verbose, including the other destinations
  • comparisons and NotNull in Ensure, whose descriptions allocate

Like RAW_VLOG, Verbose allocates and acquires a lock on the first call of a call site. Call sites that do not fit a lookup table of 4096 locations acquire a lock on every call.

With iterator debugging of the Microsoft C++ standard library, which debug builds enable by default, std::format allocates once for each integer with a format specification, such as {:#x}, and for each character or bool with an integer presentation type. Release builds do not allocate.

Floating-point arguments are formatted using std::to_chars, which never allocates, with the same output as std::format. With libstdc++, std::to_chars formats a long double with a precision or an e or g type using sprintf, which, like the prefix of RAW_LOG, is not async-signal-safe. Like its std::format, libc++ formats a long double as a double, so values beyond the range or the precision of double lose them. Their specification may contain an ASCII fill, alignment, sign, zero padding and a width of at most 512. The precision is limited to 64 and the type to a, e, f, g and their uppercase variants. Dynamic widths and precisions, the alternate form # and the fixed notation of long double, which can exceed the buffer, are rejected at compile time:

Formatting floating-point numbers
#include <ng-log/experimental/signal_safe_log.h>

ngx::Log(ngx::SignalSafe, "{:.3f} {:+e}", 3.14159, 1e300);  // compiles
ngx::Log(ngx::SignalSafe, "{:.65f}", 1.0);  // rejected: precision above 64
ngx::Log(ngx::SignalSafe, "{:f}", 1.0L);    // rejected: long double fixed

A format error detected at runtime, such as a negative dynamic width of an integer argument, throws std::format_error, which allocates.

items.title: Lazy Arguments
items.text:
Arguments are evaluated before the call even if the message is not logged. Lazy defers an expensive argument to a callable that runs only if the message is formatted, once for each replacement field that refers to it. Its result is formatted with the specification of the replacement field:

Deferring an expensive argument
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

ngx::Log(ngx::Verbose{2}, "state: {:>20}",
         ngx::Lazy([&] { return Dump(state); }));

SignalSafe does not accept lazy arguments, since the callable may allocate.

items.title: Types Without a Formatter
items.text:
The functions format the arguments of a message using std::format only. A type that supports operator<< but no formatter is logged by providing a std::formatter specialization for it:

Formatting a custom type
#include <format>

#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

struct Point {
  int x;
  int y;
};

template <>
struct std::formatter<Point> {
  constexpr auto parse(std::format_parse_context& context) {
    return context.begin();
  }

  auto format(const Point& point, std::format_context& context) const {
    return std::format_to(context.out(), "({}, {})", point.x, point.y);
  }
};

ngx::Log("Moved to {}", Point{1, 2});

items.title: Querying the Verbosity
items.text:
IsEnabled(Verbose{n}) corresponds to VLOG_IS_ON(n), which remains available. It honors --v and --vmodule with every compiler and preserves errno.

Attributes are literal types. Define them once as constexpr to use the same attributes for the query and the message:

Querying the verbosity before logging
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

constexpr auto kStatistics = ngx::Verbose{2} | ngx::Tag{"stats"};

if (ngx::IsEnabled(kStatistics)) {
  ngx::Log(kStatistics, "Statistics: {}", ComputeStatistics());
}

items.title: Attributes
items.text:
Attributes are composed with | and apply in order:

Composing attributes
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

ngx::Log(ngx::Error | ngx::Errno | ngx::Tag{"net"}, "Cannot connect to {}",
         host);
ngx::Log(ngx::Verbose{2} | ngx::Every{100}, "Processed {} items", count);

| requires at least one operand provided by ng-log. ngx::Attributes{...} composes custom attributes only:

Composing custom attributes
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

ngx::Log(ngx::Attributes{Component{"db"}, Once{}}, "Query took {}", t);

An attribute appears at most once unless it is multiple, such as ToSink, which sends the message to each of several sinks. Distinct attributes of the same category, such as Syslog and ToString, exclude each other. Compositions that violate either rule, such as ngx::Info | ngx::Warning, do not compile, and the diagnostic names the concept of the rule, SingleAttributesAreUnique or CategoriesAreDistinct. In the following table, ? means at most once and * any number of times:

Attributes Category Multiplicity Info, Warning, Error, Fatal, Severity{s} Severity ? Every, First Rate limit ? Syslog, SignalSafe Destination ? ToSink, ToString, ToVector Destination * Tag, Errno, Debug, Verbose, FatalInDebug, SkipLogFile Own ? Custom attributes Category, if declared ?, or * if Multiple

A message therefore has, for instance, a single severity and a destination of one kind, which is either Syslog or any number of sinks, strings or vectors. SkipLogFile requires at least one sink. Ensure accepts no severity.

items.title: Severity
items.text:
Attribute Effect Macro equivalent Info, Warning, Error, Fatal Logs at the severity. The default is Info. LOG(severity) FatalInDebug Raises the severity to Fatal in debug mode. none Severity{s} Logs at a runtime severity. LOG_AT_LEVEL(s)

Error | FatalInDebug behaves like LOG(DFATAL) in either order. Debug mode, which FatalInDebug depends on, and NGLOG_STRIP_LOG follow the configuration of the calling translation unit. See stripping. Unlike LOG_EVERY_N, LOG_FIRST_N, LOG_AT_LEVEL and SYSLOG, which NGLOG_STRIP_LOG does not strip, every message is stripped below the configured level regardless of its attributes.

Unlike LOG_AT_LEVEL, Severity{s} ensures that s is one of the four severities. Another value fails to compile during constant evaluation and terminates like a failed check otherwise.

items.title: Tag
Errno
items.text: Attribute Effect Macro equivalent Errno Appends : <description> [<errno>]. Captures errno before the arguments in the braced and two-stage forms. PLOG(severity)

items.title: Debug
items.text:
Attribute Effect Macro equivalent Debug Logs in debug mode only. DLOG(severity)

Debug mode follows the calling translation unit and is on unless NDEBUG is defined without DCHECK_ALWAYS_ON.

Unlike DLOG and DCHECK, whose operands disappear with the macro, the arguments of a function are evaluated in either mode. Outside debug mode, a message with Debug is neither formatted nor logged, but its arguments, the condition of Ensure and the operands of a comparison, which describes its failure, are still evaluated. Pass expensive arguments as Lazy, or skip expensive checks with if constexpr (ngx::IsDebugEnabled()).

items.title: Verbosity
items.text:
Attribute Effect Macro equivalent Verbose{n} Logs if the verbosity of the call site is at least n. VLOG(n)

Verbose derives the --vmodule module from the file name like VLOG. The level may have any standard integer type, deduced from the argument. Levels outside the range of --v saturate instead of wrapping around.

items.title: Rate Limit
Destination
items.text: Attribute Effect Macro equivalent Syslog Also logs to syslog. SYSLOG(severity) ToSink{&sink} Also logs to a sink or a structured sink. Repeat it for several sinks. LOG_TO_SINK(&sink, severity) SkipLogFile Logs to the sinks of ToSink only. Requires a sink. LOG_TO_SINK_BUT_NOT_TO_LOGFILE with ToSink ToString{&text} Also stores the text in a string. Repeat it for several strings. LOG_TO_STRING(severity, &text) ToVector{&texts} Appends the text to a vector instead of logging. Repeat it for several vectors. Null vectors are ignored, and the message is logged if all of them are null. LOG_STRING(severity, &texts)

items.title: Argument Evaluation Order
items.text:
C++ leaves the order in which the arguments of a function call are evaluated unspecified. In ngx::Log(ngx::Errno, "{}", f()), f() may run and change errno before Errno captures it, which GCC does on x86-64. Two forms enforce the order:

  • Two-stage call: ngx::Log(attributes)(format, args...). The function is evaluated before its arguments, so the logger captures the state before the arguments of the second stage. The logger can only be called right away, and discarding it without calling it is diagnosed.
  • Braces: ngx::Log{attributes, format, args...}. The elements of a braced initializer list are evaluated from left to right, so the attributes capture their state before any argument is evaluated.

MSVC

MSVC 19.51 does not evaluate braced constructor arguments from left to right, contrary to the standard. Use the two-stage form with MSVC.

Capturing errno before the arguments
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

// errno is captured before Describe(file) runs.
ngx::Log(ngx::Error | ngx::Errno)("Cannot open {}", Describe(file));
ngx::Log{ngx::Error | ngx::Errno, "Cannot open {}", Describe(file)};

Parentheses compile as well but do not enforce the order. Only attributes with a Capture hook, such as Errno, depend on it. Ensure does not enforce the order. Since Log is a class template, ngx::Log(kFormat); with a single identifier is parsed as a declaration and does not compile. Use braces in that case.

items.title: Migrating from the Macros
items.text: Conditions preferably become if statements, which also skip evaluating the arguments. ngx::Log(c, ngx::Error, "msg") corresponds to LOG_IF(ERROR, c) but evaluates the arguments regardless. Macro variants become attribute combinations. The functions below are declared in log.h, signal_safe_log.h and ensure.h of ng-log/experimental, the macros in ng-log/logging.h and ng-log/raw_logging.h. Comparisons use That. Where a failure must read exactly like the macro's, such as a == b (1 vs. 2), use NGLOG_COMPARE instead. The examples assume using namespace std::chrono_literals;.

items.title: Checks and Assertions
items.text:
The assertion macros log at the fatal severity like a failed check, so they map to Ensure, whose message starts with Check failed: instead of Assert failed:.

Macros
CHECK(p) << "msg";

PCHECK(p) << "msg";

DCHECK(p) << "msg";

CHECK_EQ(a, b) << "msg";

DCHECK_LT(i, n);


CHECK_STRCASEEQ(s1, s2);


CHECK_NEAR(x, y, m);

CHECK_DOUBLE_EQ(x, y);

CHECK_NOTNULL(p);

CHECK_INDEX(i, a);

CHECK_BOUND(b, a);

LOG_ASSERT(p);

DLOG_ASSERT(p);

SYSLOG_ASSERT(p);
Functions
ngx::Ensure(p, "p msg");

ngx::Ensure(p, ngx::Errno, "p msg");

ngx::Ensure(p, ngx::Debug, "p msg");

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(a) == b, "msg");

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(i) < n,
            ngx::Debug);

ngx::Ensure(
    ngx::That(s1).IgnoreCase() == s2);

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(x).Near(y, m));

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(x).Near(y));

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(p) != nullptr);

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(i).IndexOf(a));

ngx::Ensure(ngx::That(b).BoundOf(a));

ngx::Ensure(p, "p");

ngx::Ensure(p, ngx::Debug, "p");

ngx::Ensure(p, ngx::Syslog, "p");

items.title: Custom Attributes
items.text:
Any class type with at least one of the following const member functions is an attribute:

void Configure(nglog::experimental::Context&) const

Sets the severity, tag or other settings.

bool Admit(nglog::experimental::Context&) const

Returns false to discard the message.

bool Throttle(nglog::experimental::Context&) const

Rate limits the message. Runs after all Admit hooks passed. Returns false to discard the message.

void Prefix(nglog::experimental::Message&) const

Appends text before the formatted message.

void Suffix(nglog::experimental::Message&) const

Appends text after the formatted message.

void Fields(nglog::experimental::FieldWriter&) const

Adds fields for structured sinks. Runs only if one receives the message.

An attribute may additionally capture state at the call site:

A Capture() const

Returns a copy of the attribute A with captured state, such as errno. Runs before the arguments are evaluated in the braced and two-stage forms of Log. Otherwise it runs in unspecified order relative to the arguments, and after them in Ensure.

Hooks run in phases, each in composition order:

flowchart TB
  subgraph admission [Admission]
    direction LR
    Capture --> Configure --> Admit --> Throttle
  end
  subgraph message [Message]
    direction LR
    Fields --> Prefix --> Format --> Suffix
  end
  admission --> message

A false from Admit or Throttle discards the message. Stripping is checked after Admit and --minloglevel after Throttle, so rate limits count suppressed messages like the macros do. Arguments are formatted only if the message is logged. IsEnabled runs Configure and Admit only.

A member type Category makes distinct attributes of that category exclusive. An attribute appears at most once in a composition unless it declares using Multiplicity = ngx::Multiple;.

Context provides the severity, tag, debug mode and call site location. Its setters change the severity, the tag and the errno the message reports. site() returns per-site state, created on first use, alive until program exit and shared across threads. Message appends text and provides the errno the message reports. Its out() returns an output iterator, so std::format_to(message.out(), ...) formats without a temporary string.

Examples that prepend a component, gate on a switch and log a site once:

Defining custom attributes
#include <atomic>
#include <format>
#include <string_view>

#include <ng-log/experimental/attributes.h>
#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>

struct Component {
  std::string_view name;

  void Prefix(ngx::Message& message) const {
    std::format_to(message.out(), "[{}] ", name);
  }
};

struct Switch {
  const std::atomic<bool>* on;

  bool Admit(ngx::Context&) const {
    return on->load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
  }
};

struct Once {
  struct State {
    std::atomic_flag logged;
  };

  bool Throttle(ngx::Context& context) const {
    return !context.site().state<State>().logged.test_and_set(
        std::memory_order_relaxed);
  }
};

ngx::Log(ngx::Warning | Component{"net"} | Once{}, "Retrying");

items.title: Structured Sinks
items.text:
A nglog::LogSink receives the formatted text only. A structured ngx::Sink receives an ngx::Record, which also provides the location of the call including the function, the tag, the time as std::chrono::sys_time with the UTC offset of the log files, and the fields the attributes contribute through their Fields hook. This suits structured logging systems such as journald. ToSink sends a message to either kind of sink:

Sending messages to a structured sink
#include <array>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <ostream>
#include <print>
#include <string_view>
#include <utility>

#include <ng-log/experimental/log.h>
#include <ng-log/experimental/sink.h>

// Writes the fields of a message in the journal export format.
class JournalSink final : public ngx::Sink {
 public:
  void Send(const ngx::Record& record) override {
    // Syslog priorities of the severities INFO, WARNING, ERROR and FATAL.
    constexpr std::array kPriorities{6, 4, 3, 2};
    const auto time =
        std::chrono::floor<std::chrono::microseconds>(record.time());
    std::print(
        std::cout,
        "MESSAGE={}\nPRIORITY={}\nCODE_FILE={}\nCODE_LINE={}\nCODE_FUNC={}\n"
        "__REALTIME_TIMESTAMP={}\n",
        record.text(), kPriorities[static_cast<std::size_t>(std::to_underlying(record.severity()))],
        record.location().file_name(), record.location().line(),
        record.location().function_name(), time.time_since_epoch().count());
    for (const ngx::Field& field : record.fields()) {
      std::print(std::cout, "{}={}\n", field.name, field.value);
    }
    std::print(std::cout, "\n");
  }
};

// Adds the component as a field.
struct ComponentField {
  std::string_view name;

  void Fields(ngx::FieldWriter& fields) const { fields.Add("COMPONENT", name); }
};

JournalSink journal;
ngx::Log(ngx::Warning | ngx::ToSink{&journal} | ComponentField{"db"},
         "Retrying");

std::print requires C++23. With C++20, std::format_to(std::ostreambuf_iterator<char>{std::cout}, ...) writes the same text, and unlike std::print without formatting into a temporary string first. A record and its fields are valid only while the sink receives them. If the standard library provides the time zone database, which __cpp_lib_chrono indicates with 201907L or later, zoned_time() returns the time as std::chrono::zoned_time in the time zone of the log files. time_zone() returns that zone, which is UTC if --log_utc_time is set and the current zone otherwise. Without the database, time(), utc_offset() and utc() provide the same information. Combined with SkipLogFile, the message reaches the sinks only.

items.title: Differences from the Macros
items.text:
Messages are formatted identically. Behavior differs as follows:

  • The functions define no unprefixed macros and do not conflict with other logging libraries. The macros do.
  • Arguments are always evaluated, also for a condition of Log that does not hold or a check that passes. Only formatting is skipped. Use Lazy to defer expensive arguments or an if statement to log conditionally.
  • Errno captures errno before the arguments are evaluated only in the braced and two-stage forms. PLOG always does.
  • Ensure, That and the comparison functions cannot capture the expression text. Use NGLOG_COMPARE or pass it explicitly.
  • Comparisons of integers with mixed signedness compare by value.
  • Rate limits and verbosity keep their state per call site, which is identified by file, function, line and column instead of a static variable.
  • Verbose and IsEnabled honor --vmodule with every compiler. The macros honor it only with compilers that support GNU extensions.
  • NGLOG_STRIP_LOG suppresses messages but keeps format strings in the binary.
  • SignalSafe accepts fewer argument types than RAW_LOG and restricts the specification of floating-point arguments.
  • Types are formatted using a std::formatter instead of operator<<. See types without a formatter.
